recipe.history:
Muenster cheese traces its origins to the Alsace region straddling the border of modern-day France and Germany, where Benedictine monks in the Vosges Mountains began crafting it as early as the 7th century AD. Named after the town of Munster — derived from the Latin "monasterium," meaning monastery — the original fromage de Munster was a washed-rind cheese with a pungent, orange-hued rind and a supple, ivory interior. The monks washed the rind in brine, wine, or beer during aging, which encouraged the growth of Brevibacterium linens and gave the cheese its characteristic earthy aroma and buttery, slightly tangy flavor. Over centuries, it became a staple of Alsatian farmhouse tables, served alongside charcuterie, rye bread, and cumin seeds — a combination still considered traditional in the region today.

When European immigrants arrived on American shores in the 18th and 19th centuries, they brought their cheesemaking traditions with them. German and French settlers adapted old-world techniques to the milder climates and different milk supplies of the American Midwest, and in doing so, invented what we now call American Muenster — a far gentler cousin to its European ancestor. Shorn of its pungent rind and aged for a shorter period, American Muenster became a semi-soft, mild, supremely meltable cheese with a pale yellow interior and an orange-colored rind achieved through annatto coloring rather than bacterial washing. Its extraordinary melting properties made it a natural fit for the American hamburger tradition, which was itself taking shape in diners and lunch counters across the country in the early 20th century. By mid-century, Muenster had earned its place among the great burger cheeses — not as flashy as a sharp cheddar, not as pedestrian as American singles, but quietly, dependably perfect.

I remember the first time I truly understood what a Muenster burger could be. It was late October, the kind of evening where the air smells like wood smoke and dying leaves, and I was sitting in a vinyl booth at a roadside diner somewhere outside of Pittsburgh. The place had no pretensions — laminated menus, a pie case with one sad slice of cherry left in it, a counterman who called everyone "hon." But the burger that arrived in front of me was something else entirely: a thick, hand-formed patty under a molten blanket of Muenster that had gone completely translucent at the edges, pooling into the toasted bun like warm velvet. I didn't say anything for a long moment. I just ate. Outside, a truck rumbled past and the neon sign buzzed in the window, and I thought: this is exactly what a burger is supposed to be. Not a statement. Not a spectacle. Just meat and cheese and bread, each element doing its job with quiet excellence.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef patty, and that temperature is medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a matter of preference; it is a matter of physics, chemistry, and respect for the animal. At medium rare, the myoglobin in the beef has not fully denatured, leaving the center a warm, rosy pink with a yielding, almost custardy texture. The fat within the grind has begun to render but has not been cooked away, meaning every bite carries the full, rounded flavor of the beef rather than a dry, gray approximation of it. The Maillard reaction on the exterior crust is at its peak — deeply browned, slightly crisp, intensely savory — while the interior remains tender and juicy. To cook a burger beyond this point is to chase moisture and flavor out of the meat and replace them with nothing. A well-done burger is not a safe burger; it is a surrendered one. Cook your patty to medium rare, let it rest, and serve it immediately. Everything else is a footnote.
ingredients: 360g bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 egg yolk + 1 tbsp heavy cream (egg wash)
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef — 70% chuck, 30% short rib blend
4 thick slices (approx. 30g each) American-style Muenster cheese
Salt and white pepper to taste
240ml neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola)
1 head butter lettuce, leaves separated and washed
2 large ripe beefsteak tomatoes, sliced 1/4-inch thick
1 large white onion, thinly sliced into rings
8 bread-and-butter pickle chips (homemade or quality store-bought)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook, combine bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to combine dry ingredients. Add eggs and warm milk, mixing on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.

2. Increase mixer to medium speed and knead dough for 8 minutes until it begins to pull away from the sides of the bowl. With the mixer running on medium-low, add softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to be fully incorporated before adding the next. This process takes 10–12 minutes. The finished dough will be glossy, smooth, and slightly tacky.
3. Shape dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–16 hours). Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the dough easier to shape.

4. The next day, remove dough from refrigerator and allow to rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Shape each into a tight ball by folding the edges under and rolling against the counter with a cupped hand. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet spaced 3 inches apart. Flatten each ball gently to about 1 inch thick.

5. Cover loosely with a damp kitchen towel and proof at room temperature until doubled and pillowy, 2–3 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Whisk together egg yolk and heavy cream for egg wash. Brush buns gently with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.

6. Bake for 16–18 minutes, rotating the pan once halfway through, until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing. Do not rush this step — cutting a warm brioche bun compresses it and ruins the texture.

7. MAKE THE HOMEMADE MAYONNAISE: Place egg yolks, Dijon mustard, and white wine vinegar in a medium bowl. Whisk vigorously for 1 minute until the yolks are pale and slightly thickened. Begin adding the neutral oil drop by drop while whisking constantly. Once an emulsion has formed (after about 3 tablespoons of oil), you may increase to a thin, steady stream. Continue whisking until all oil is incorporated and the mayonnaise is thick and glossy. Season with lemon juice and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

8. MAKE THE SPECIAL SAUCE: In a bowl, combine 120ml of the homemade mayonnaise with ketchup, yellow mustard, sweet pickle relish, apple cider vinegar, smoked paprika, onion powder, garlic powder, and cayenne. Whisk until smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and white pepper. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

9. MAKE CARAMELIZED ONIONS (optional but highly recommended): In a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet over medium-low heat, melt butter with olive oil. Add sliced yellow onions and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 5–7 minutes, for 45–60 minutes until the onions are deeply golden, jammy, and sweet. Add brown sugar and balsamic vinegar in the last 5 minutes, stirring to glaze. Remove from heat and set aside.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Gently divide the beef into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Using as little pressure as possible — overworking the meat compacts it and toughens the texture — form each portion into a patty about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb (this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks). Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking. Do not season in advance.

11. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy stainless steel pan over high heat until smoking — approximately 5 minutes on a gas burner. Do not use nonstick. Add a thin film of neutral oil to the pan. Place patties in the pan, dimple-side up, without pressing them down. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to build a deep, dark sear.

12. Flip patties once. Immediately add butter, smashed garlic cloves, and fresh thyme sprigs to the pan. As the butter melts and foams, tilt the pan and use a large spoon to continuously baste the top of each patty with the hot flavored butter. Cook for an additional 2 minutes while basting.

13. Check internal temperature using an instant-read thermometer inserted into the side of each patty. Target temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare — a warm, rosy-pink center. Remove patties from heat at 128°F (53°C) if carryover cooking is a concern. Transfer to a wire rack set over a plate to rest. Do not place on a flat surface — resting on a rack prevents the bottom from steaming and losing its crust.

14. MELT THE MUENSTER: Immediately after removing patties from heat and while they rest on the rack, lay one thick slice of Muenster over each patty. Tent loosely with aluminum foil for 2 minutes. The residual heat will melt the Muenster into a glossy, completely molten layer. If you require more aggressive melting, use a dome lid over the patties in the pan with 1 tablespoon of water for a brief steam — 30 seconds maximum.

15. TOAST THE BUNS: Wipe the cast iron pan clean and return it to medium heat. Spread a thin layer of softened butter on the cut face of each bun half. Place cut-side down in the dry pan and toast for 90 seconds until golden brown with lightly crisped edges. Do not walk away — brioche burns faster than standard buns.

16. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Work quickly and deliberately. Spread a generous tablespoon of special sauce on the cut face of the bottom bun. Layer with 2 butter lettuce leaves, 2 slices of beefsteak tomato (lightly salted), and 3–4 rings of raw white onion. Place the Muenster-topped patty on the onion rings. Add a spoonful of caramelized onions if using, and 2 pickle chips. Spread another tablespoon of special sauce on the cut face of the top bun. Set the top bun in place. Do not press the burger down.

17. REST AND SERVE: Allow the assembled burger to rest for 60 seconds before serving. This allows the juices that redistributed during the patty's rest to settle into the bun. Serve immediately on a warmed plate. The internal temperature of the patty at the moment of eating should be between 125–130°F (52–54°C) — perfectly medium rare, pink throughout, juicy, and complete.
